source.title: Superposition Yields Robust Neural Scaling
source.authors: Yizhou Liu; Zi-Ming Liu; Jeff Gore

record.file_problem: None; the full paper, appendices, and checklist are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how loss scaling changes with superposition and data-frequency distributions, refining the scope of power-law claims. It also measures held-out losses for open-source language models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports toy-model loss scaling and evaluations of LLM loss against model dimension. It also measures representation overlaps, recorded separately as a finding not covered by the listed claim versions. Token-frequency measurements and the Chinchilla parameter-count conversion are explanatory or derived inputs, not separate loss-scaling results here; results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates held-out loss of existing open LLMs (OPT, Qwen2.5, GPT-2, Pythia; about 100M–70B) on four text datasets. It fits loss against model width as a power law plus a constant. That is a different method, observational across released models, aimed at V1's model-size power law. The toy-autoencoder sweeps are a mechanistic model, not language-model pretraining loss, so they bear on no listed version directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. Authors conclude that representation superposition is a central driver of neural scaling. Under strong superposition, toy loss scales about 1/m robustly across frequency distributions. Under weak superposition, a power law appears only if feature frequencies are power-law. Open LLMs are in strong superposition, with token frequencies α≈1 and loss scaling close to 1/m (αm=0.91±0.04). Chinchilla's model-size exponent, converted via N∝m^2.52, gives a consistent αm≈0.88.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an autoencoder toy model with synthetic feature-frequency distributions to study width scaling, then evaluates existing LLMs on text datasets. It does not reproduce the original parameter/data/compute sweeps or fixed-compute allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Toy-model scaling depends on superposition (controlled by weight decay) and feature-frequency distribution/exponent. The reported power-law fit procedure selects different portions of curves in different conditions; the LLM fit includes separate constants for each dataset and model class.

fits_no_version.finding: In a toy ReLU autoencoder, strong superposition gives reconstruction loss ∝ about 1/m across exponential, power-law and linear feature frequencies (αm ≈ 0.89–1.01). Weak superposition gives power-law loss only for power-law feature frequencies (αm ≈ α−1). Skewed frequencies under strong superposition raise αm toward 2(α−1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy representation models, whether loss is a power law in width, and its exponent, depend on degree of superposition and on the feature-frequency distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean squared overlap of normalized LM-head rows in open LLMs roughly scales as 1/m (noisy, not fitted).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In studied LLM families, representation-vector overlap decreases roughly inversely with model dimension and may contribute to width-related loss scaling.

record.problems: The authors say they do not rigorously solve the toy model. The LLM-to-token-feature mapping is described as naive, and the LLM loss analysis is observational rather than a controlled training sweep. The LLM fit has 18 parameters for 16 model-class/dataset combinations; the raw loss plots are described as noisy. Power-law fits use selected curve ranges in some toy conditions, and the paper notes that some curves are not well described by a power law.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately reported loss-scaling outcomes omitted. Token-frequency distributions and derived parameter-count conversions are not separate loss results; cited scaling exponents are not treated as this study's measurements.

untested.parts: Scaling in training tokens and in compute. No controlled sweep: models come from different families with different data and token budgets, so 'other factors not the bottleneck' is unverified. Width spans about one order of magnitude.
All: no extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
All: depth/width trade-off only discussed speculatively (Eq. 7).
Not tested on language models. The LLM fit imposes a shared exponent. The dependence of exponents on data distribution and regime is shown only in toy autoencoders.

record.verdict_notes: The Chinchilla-derived αm = 0.88 ± 0.06 combines a cited αN (Besiroglu et al.) with the study's own N–m fit. It is a derived, not measured, loss result and correctly is not a row. The toy results are relabelled to 'none' because the system and loss (autoencoder MSE) differ from V1/V7's language-model pretraining loss. If the phenomenon file treats toy models as in scope for V7, R1–R7 would bear on V7 as showing exponent and form depending on data distribution and superposition.

versions.untested_parts: The toy-model sweeps test loss against model dimension; the LLM evaluation fits loss against model dimension and relates dimension to parameter count. The paper does not directly sweep training-token count or training compute.
No prediction from fits on small runs to substantially larger runs is tested.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling results are tested.
No downstream-task performance or its predictability from scale or pretraining loss is tested.

The study tests dependence on superposition, feature-frequency distribution, and fit choices. It does not test compute-optimal allocation dependence or independently compare published laws under matched setups.

rows.subject: small toy models
rows.size_stated: data dimension n = 1000; model dimensions m = 10, 15, 25, 39, 63, 100
rows.operation_detail: Scanned data exponent α and weight decay γ; fitted loss against model dimension.

conditions.value: power law, pi ∝ 1/i^α; α scanned from 0 to 2

rows.measure: Fitted model exponent αm and fit quality for loss versus model dimension.
rows.value: Under strong superposition αm stays near 1 across a range of small α and increases with α for large α; under weak superposition αm is small. The paper reports that some weak-superposition fits, especially at large γ, are not good power laws.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars are standard errors in Figures 9b and 10.
rows.note: The paper fits a power law in all cases to extract αm, but notes that some curves are not well described by that form.
rows.check: Toy autoencoder sweep, not an LM. 'Partial' describes the toy fit quality across γ and α, not any version's effect.

rows.subject: OPT, Qwen2.5, GPT-2, and Pythia models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Around 100M to 70B in the reported evaluation; appendix lists OPT-125m to OPT-66b, Qwen2.5 0.5B to 72B, GPT-2 through GPT2-XL, and Pythia 70m to 12B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated models on four text datasets and fitted a shared loss-versus-dimension power law with dataset- and model-class-specific constants.

conditions.value: Four model classes; shared fit across 16 model-class/dataset combinations

rows.measure: Held-out evaluation loss fitted as L = Cm/m^αm + L\m.
rows.uncertainty: ±0.04; uncertainty type for this fitted exponent is not stated.
rows.note: The fit uses 18 parameters, including 16 constants for model class and dataset. The paper says the loss-versus-1/m plots are noisy and does not fit the overlap plot with a line.
rows.check: Linked to V1 only. The fit uses one shared exponent across model classes and datasets, so it cannot show exponent dependence on setup (V7). Models differ in training data and token counts, which is uncontrolled. Width spans only about one order of magnitude. Each class/dataset pair gets its own constant offset, and the raw plots are described as noisy.

rows.subject: OPT, Qwen2.5, GPT-2, and Pythia models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Model families spanning the sizes listed in Appendix C.1
rows.operation_detail: Measured pairwise overlaps among normalized language-model-head rows.
rows.measure: Mean squared overlap of normalized rows versus model dimension.
rows.value: The mean squared overlaps roughly follow 1/m; the plotted data are described as noisy.
rows.note: This is a proposed mechanism for loss scaling, not a loss measurement itself.

relationships.condition: Open pretrained LLMs (OPT, Qwen2.5, GPT-2, Pythia), evaluated on Wikitext-103, Pile-10k, C4 and BookCorpus
relationships.reason: Held-out loss fits L = Cm/m^αm + const with αm = 0.91 ± 0.04, and raw losses look linear in 1/m (R8). This is observational, with per-class/dataset offsets.
relationships.display_finding: Observed held-out loss fitted L = Cₘ/m^αₘ + constant with αₘ = 0.91 ± 0.04 and family/dataset-specific offsets, while raw loss appeared approximately linear in 1/m.
